summary:
EVKIWI by Team Cosmosaver (Jiaqi, Edward, Marco) is an on-board AI health monitor that gives astronauts extra safe hours on spacewalks.

During an EVA, the drop in suit pressure can cause decompression sickness. Today’s protocols are one-size-fits-all and often cut walks short, and on Mars, help from Earth is up to 24 minutes away. EVKIWI combines a 10-second breath test (DLCO), hydration, fatigue, bubble grade and training load into one decompression risk score (GREEN to RED). It then gives personalised recommendation cards, such as a longer prebreathe, moving heavy exercise or rehydrating, and each card shows how many safe EVA hours it adds.

A 3D spacewalk on the ISS, the Moon and Mars shows the impact: with the recommendations accepted, the astronaut finishes the full walk instead of returning early. Astronauts get a simple daily dashboard and calendar, and mission planners see the whole crew and approve plans.

Work longer, smarter, safer
details:
EVKIWI: Extra safe hours outside

Team Cosmosaver (Jiaqi, Edward, Marco), for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

The problem

Spacewalks (EVAs) are some of the most valuable and most dangerous hours of a mission. Astronauts move from cabin pressure into a low-pressure suit. Nitrogen dissolved in their tissues can form bubbles, which causes decompression sickness (DCS): joint pain, breathing problems and, in severe cases, neurological damage. Today, risk is managed with fixed, conservative protocols such as long oxygen prebreathes that treat every astronaut the same. That keeps people safe, but it costs time, and a walk often ends early because no one can see each astronaut’s real risk in the moment.

The problem grows on the way to the Moon and Mars. A Mars signal takes 4 to 24 minutes each way, so real-time help from flight surgeons on Earth isn’t possible. Crews need a tool on board that judges their readiness and tells them what to do.

Our solution

EVKIWI is an AI health monitor for EVA readiness and decompression stress. It runs on board without needing Earth and syncs later. It combines each astronaut’s physiological data into one decompression risk score (DRI) with a clear status: GREEN, YELLOW, ORANGE or RED.

Inputs include:

  • Lung function (DLCO): a short 10-second breath test that shows how well the lungs clear gas.
  • Hydration and fatigue, which strongly affect bubble formation.
  • Bubble grade from ultrasound, and symptoms the astronaut reports.
  • Training load: heavy resistance exercise close to an EVA increases risk.

EVKIWI goes beyond a score. It gives recommendation cards, such as extending the prebreathe, moving heavy exercise away from the EVA day, or rehydrating. Each card shows how many safe EVA hours it adds. The headline number, “+X h safe EVA time this mission”, grows as the crew accepts recommendations. Our value: give NASA’s astronauts extra hours outside while protecting their health, so they work longer, smarter and safer.

How it works

  1. Measure: the astronaut does the breath test and logs how they feel.
  2. Score: the model combines the inputs into the DRI and explains “why this score”.
  3. Recommend: personalised cards with Accept and Snooze. Accepted cards update the plan.
  4. Simulate: a 3D spacewalk shows the effect. On a YELLOW day without recommendations, the astronaut has to come back after 4.5 hours. With the cards accepted, they finish the full walk and gain about +4.3 hours of safe EVA time. On RED, the walk is aborted.
  5. Debrief: after the walk comes a DCS test with a score dial and new recommendations, including rescheduling any skipped tasks.

The experience

  • Immersive landing: a 3D hologram astronaut in kiwi green climbs out of the hatch and along the station, with organs and joints glowing as risk changes. The scene tours the ISS, the Moon and Mars.
  • Full mission simulation: suit-up and prebreathe, then real tasks (sample collection, drilling, station setup), with a “Return to ship” button that works at any moment. It ends with the DCS test back inside.
    • Astronaut: a calm, easy home screen with today’s status in one word, ready-made graphs (bone density, heart rate and HRV, hydration, DLCO, radiation) and a week calendar where suggestions can be accepted with one tap.
    • Mission planner: the whole crew at a glance, with alerts, a 7-day EVA and training timeline that flags clashes, approval of recommendations, and links to every detailed tool.

Who it’s for

  • Astronauts, who want more productive, safer time outside.
  • Flight surgeons, who need objective readiness data.
  • Mission planners, who schedule EVAs, exercise and rest.
  • Space agencies and commercial stations, where every EVA hour is expensive.

Why it matters

Each extra safe EVA hour means more science, more maintenance and more exploration from missions that cost billions. Personalised, explainable recommendations turn a one-size-fits-all protocol into adaptive care, and they keep working where Earth can’t help in real time.

Technology

  • Web front end with a 3D scene (WebGL) and a minimalist, premium hologram style.
  • Python (FastAPI) backend with a DCS risk model, plus a built-in fallback model so the demo also runs as a static site.
  • Hosted on GitHub Pages and redeployed on every update.
  • Demo data and hour values are illustrative. They show the concept and are not clinical results.

What’s next

Validate the model against published NASA DCS and prebreathe data, connect real wearables and the breath sensor, and run trials in analog missions on the way to lunar EVAs.

Check the hour figures and the technical claims against your own model before you submit.
dataRefs: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes
